name: Ostensive NP

dimensions.form: Extra-clausal NP with marked prosody; NP-internal licensing is preserved but differs between vocative and directive-ostensive packaging
dimensions.meaning: Directs attention to a referent (addressee or environmental)
dimensions.function: Attention-securing utterance; not an argument of any predicator
dimensions.distribution: Stand-alone or supplement position; resists embedding, tags, and questioning

1.definition: An extra-clausal NP whose utterance directs attention to its referent, with packaging-specific NP-internal syntax preserved
1.details: The structural parent of vocative-001 (addressee-directed: securing the channel) and directive-ostensive-001 (environment-directed: securing joint attention). Ordinary determination applies in the directive-ostensive packaging, while vocative function independently licenses bare common-noun NPs such as Mum, driver, officer, and buddy (CGEL pp. 522–23). The packagings shade into each other: Taxi! is ambiguous between hailing the driver and alerting companions, and reminders (Your keys!) sit between alerting and addressing. The construction cross-cuts exclamation-001: tag vocatives instantiate this profile without exclamatory force.

examples.note: Boundary case, ambiguous between the two packagings

constraints.description: Determination is packaging-sensitive: directive-ostensives preserve ordinary determination (a snake, the bus), while vocative function licenses restricted bare common-noun NPs (Mum, driver, buddy).
Not selected by any predicator; resists embedding, tags, and question formation.

projection.target: Membership predicts packaging-specific NP syntax despite extra-clausal status, introduction of a discourse referent available to anaphora, an orientation-type rather than verbal response, and marked prosody
projection.evidence: Directive-ostensives preserve ordinary determination where block language sheds it, while vocatives license a restricted bare-NP inventory (CGEL pp. 522–23); both packagings retain referential and orientation behaviour unlike interjections

diagnostics: licensed bare common nouns in vocatives

stabilisers.evidence: Attention-securing must be fast; minimal structure with maximal prosodic salience
Plausibly continuous with pre-linguistic pointing and the one-word stage; testable in CHILDES

known_boundary_items: block language (form without prosody or determination)
clausal alerts (There's a fire!: function without the form)

grounds.note: Vocative function licenses restricted bare common-noun NPs

curious.title: A single noun phrase that calls for attention
curious.summary: A lone noun phrase, said with marked stress, can direct someone's attention to a person or thing.
curious.body: Sometimes a single noun phrase is a complete message. Calling Mom! gets the listener's attention. Pointing out A snake! gets everyone's attention for something in the surroundings. Both are said with marked stress and aren't part of a longer sentence. This dictionary separates two uses: calling to the person addressed, and drawing attention to something in the environment. They shade into each other. Taxi! could hail the driver or alert a friend. The phrase resists being questioned, tagged or tucked inside another sentence.
curious.try: Think of something you might shout in a crowd, like a name or a thing. Is it calling a person or pointing something out?

teacher.summary: Shows how a single noun phrase can serve as an attention-directing utterance, with two packagings that differ in determination.
teacher.explain: An ostensive NP is an extra-clausal NP that directs attention to its referent. It isn't an argument of any predicator, and it resists embedding, tags and question formation. It has two packagings: vocative (addressee-directed, securing the channel) and directive-ostensive (environment-directed, securing joint attention). Directive-ostensives keep ordinary determination (a snake, the bus), while vocative function licenses restricted bare common-noun NPs (Mum, driver, officer, buddy). Taxi! is ambiguous between the two, and reminders such as Your keys! sit between alerting and addressing. This dictionary marks the analysis as provisional.
teacher.terms: The addressee-directed use is the vocative. Directive-ostensive is this dictionary's term for the environment-directed use.

contrasts.note: Vocative, a bare common noun allowed in calling.
A clausal alert, which has the function but not this form.

watch_for: A learner might think a vocative such as Mum needs a determiner like a or the.
A learner might take Taxi! as having one fixed use, when it is ambiguous between the two.
A learner might treat a lone noun phrase as an interjection, when it keeps its referential behaviour.
teacher.activity: Students list short shouts from a playground or street scene. They decide for each whether it calls a person (vocative) or points something out (directive-ostensive), and mark the ambiguous ones.

child.hook: What do you shout when you see a snake?
child.explain: Sometimes just a name or a thing is the whole message. A snake! tells everyone to look. Mom! calls someone over. You don't need a verb.
child.play: Take turns shouting just a thing or a name. Can your friend tell whether you're calling someone or pointing something out?
